questions.q: Explain the CSS box model and what box-sizing: border-box changes.
questions.answer:
**Every element is a box made of content, padding, border and margin. By default (`content-box`) `width` sets only the content, so padding and border are added on top; with `box-sizing: border-box`, `width` includes padding and border, which makes sizing predictable.**

**The layers, inside out**
- **Content:** where text and children go.
- **Padding:** space inside the border; takes the element's background.
- **Border:** drawn around the padding.
- **Margin:** transparent space outside; vertical margins between blocks can collapse.

```css
.a { box-sizing: content-box; width: 200px; padding: 20px; border: 5px solid; }
/* rendered width = 200 + 2*20 + 2*5 = 250px */

.b { box-sizing: border-box; width: 200px; padding: 20px; border: 5px solid; }
/* rendered width = 200px, content shrinks to 150px */
```

**Why everyone resets it**

```css
*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }
```

With `border-box`, a `width: 50%` column with padding still fits two per row; with `content-box` it overflows and wraps. Almost every reset (and Tailwind's preflight) applies this.

**Gotchas**
- Margins are never part of the width in either mode.
- Inline elements (`<span>`) ignore `width`/`height` and vertical margins; use `inline-block` or flex/grid if you need them.
- Outline and box-shadow do not take up space at all, which is why they are good for focus rings.
followUps: What is margin collapse and when does it happen?
What is the difference between outline and border?
How do inline, inline-block and block elements differ in how they treat the box model?
mistakes: Forgetting that border is included in border-box width, not just padding.
Thinking margin is included in width under border-box.
Not knowing inline elements ignore width, height and vertical margin.

questions.q: How does the CSS cascade decide which rule wins? Explain specificity and cascade layers (@layer).
questions.answer:
**The cascade picks a winner per property by checking, in order: origin and `!important`, cascade layer, specificity, and finally source order. Specificity only matters once two declarations are in the same origin and layer.**

**The order of checks**
1. **Origin and importance:** user-agent, user, author styles; `!important` flips the order.
2. **Context:** styles inside a shadow tree vs outside.
3. **Inline `style` attribute** beats selector-based rules.
4. **Cascade layers:** later-declared layers win; unlayered styles beat all layered styles.
5. **Specificity:** (ids, classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, elements/pseudo-elements), compared left to right.
6. **Source order:** last one wins.

```css
#nav .link      /* (1,1,0) */
.nav a:hover    /* (0,2,1) */
a               /* (0,0,1) */
```

`#nav .link` wins because one id beats any number of classes. `:where()` has zero specificity; `:is()` and `:not()` take the specificity of their most specific argument.

**Cascade layers fix specificity wars**

```css
@layer reset, vendor, components, utilities;

@layer vendor { #app .btn { color: gray; } }
@layer utilities { .text-red { color: red; } }
```

`.text-red` wins even though its specificity is lower, because `utilities` is declared after `vendor`. This lets you drop a third-party stylesheet into a low layer and override it with simple classes instead of `!important` or id selectors.

**Gotchas**
- Unlayered CSS beats every layer, which surprises people adopting layers gradually.
- `!important` reverses layer order: an important declaration in an *earlier* layer wins.
- Inheritance is not the cascade: an inherited value loses to any rule that targets the element directly, even `*`.
followUps: What is the specificity of `:is(#a, .b) span` and of `:where(#a) span`?
How does !important interact with cascade layers?
How would you introduce @layer into a large existing codebase?
mistakes: Treating specificity as a base-10 number (11 classes do not beat one id).
Forgetting that unlayered styles beat all layered styles.
Confusing inheritance with the cascade.

questions.q: Explain the position values and stacking contexts. Why does z-index: 9999 sometimes not work?
questions.answer:
**`z-index` only orders elements within the same stacking context. If an element sits inside a parent that created its own stacking context, it can never appear above something outside that parent, no matter how high its z-index.** **Position values** - `static`: normal flow; `top`/`z-index` ignored. - `relative`: normal flow, offset visually, becomes a containing block for absolute children. - `absolute`: removed from flow, positioned against the nearest positioned ancestor. - `fixed`: positioned against the viewport (unless an ancestor has `transform`, `filter` or `contain`, which traps it). - `sticky`: flows normally until a scroll threshold, then sticks within its scroll container. **What creates a stacking context** (common ones) - Root element; `position` other than static with a `z-index` other than auto; `position: fixed` or `sticky`. - `opacity` below 1, `transform`, `filter`, `backdrop-filter`, `mix-blend-mode`. - Flex or grid children with a `z-index`; `isolation: isolate`; `will-change` on those properties; `contain: paint`. ```html
Menu
Content
``` The dropdown is trapped inside the header's context (z 1), so `main` (z 2) covers it. Fix: raise the header, remove the parent's context, or render the dropdown at the top level (a portal, or the native popover API / ``, which use the browser's top layer). **Gotchas** - A `transform` added for an animation silently creates a context and breaks a child `position: fixed`. - `sticky` fails if an ancestor has `overflow: hidden`. - Use `isolation: isolate` deliberately on components so their internal z-indexes never leak.

mistakes: Believing a higher z-index always wins globally.
Not knowing transform or opacity create a stacking context.
Forgetting z-index has no effect on statically positioned non-flex elements.

questions.q: Explain CSS units: px, em, rem, %, vw/vh and dvh. When do you use each?
questions.answer:
**`px` is fixed, `rem` is relative to the root font size, `em` to the current element's font size, `%` to the parent (for width) and viewport units to the screen. Use `rem` for type and spacing so everything scales with the user's font setting, and `dvh` instead of `vh` for full-height mobile layouts.**

**Each unit**
- **`px`:** borders, hairlines, shadows. Does not scale with the browser font-size preference.
- **`rem`:** font sizes, spacing, breakpoints. Respects user zoom and accessibility settings.
- **`em`:** things that should scale with their own text, like a button's padding or an icon next to text. Compounds when nested.
- **`%`:** width relative to the containing block; note `padding-top: 50%` is relative to the parent's *width*.
- **`vw` / `vh`:** viewport size; `100vw` includes the scrollbar and can cause horizontal overflow.
- **`dvh` / `svh` / `lvh`:** dynamic, small and large viewport heights, which account for mobile browser toolbars appearing and hiding.
- **`ch`:** width of "0", great for line length (`max-width: 65ch`).

```css
html { font-size: 100%; }          /* keep user default, usually 16px */
h1 { font-size: clamp(1.75rem, 1rem + 3vw, 3rem); }
.btn { padding: .5em 1em; }        /* scales with button text */
.hero { min-height: 100dvh; }      /* no jump under mobile URL bar */
.prose { max-width: 65ch; }
```

**Gotchas**
- `em` compounds: a `1.2em` list inside a `1.2em` list is 1.44 times bigger.
- `100vh` on iOS is the large viewport, so content hides under the toolbar; that is why `dvh` exists.
- Setting `html { font-size: 62.5% }` to do pixel math works but fights users who changed their default font size less gracefully than just using rem.
- Pure `vw` font sizes break zoom; always mix with rem in `clamp()`.
followUps: Why should breakpoints use rem or em rather than px?

mistakes: Not knowing em compounds through nesting.
Using 100vh for mobile full-screen layouts.

questions.q: What is a block formatting context (BFC) and how does it relate to margin collapse?
questions.answer:
**A block formatting context is an independent layout region where block boxes are laid out vertically and floats are contained. Vertical margins collapse between blocks in the same BFC; creating a new BFC stops a parent's margin from collapsing with its children and makes it wrap its floats.** **Margin collapse rules** - Adjacent vertical margins of block siblings collapse to the larger one (20px and 30px give 30px, not 50px). - A parent's top margin collapses with its first child's top margin if nothing separates them (no border, padding, inline content or BFC). The child's margin then "leaks" out of the parent. - Empty blocks collapse their own top and bottom margins. - Horizontal margins never collapse, and margins never collapse inside flex or grid containers. ```html

Title

``` ```css .card { background: #eee; } /* The 24px pushes .card down instead of creating space inside it. */ .card { display: flow-root; } /* new BFC: margin stays inside */ ``` **Ways to create a BFC** - `display: flow-root` (the clean, purpose-built one) - `overflow` other than visible (side effect: clipping) - Floats, absolutely positioned elements, `inline-block` - Flex and grid items, `contain: layout` or `paint` **Why it still matters:** the classic "clearfix" for floats is just a BFC; `flow-root` replaced the `::after { clear: both }` hack. Margin leaks cause real bugs in component libraries, which is one reason many design systems use `gap` in flex/grid instead of margins for spacing.
followUps: Why do margins not collapse inside a flex container?
What is the clearfix hack and what replaced it?
How does using gap avoid margin issues?
mistakes: Thinking collapsed margins add together.
Not knowing a child margin can escape its parent.
Using overflow: hidden to create a BFC without realising it clips content and shadows.

questions.q: How are CSS custom properties different from Sass or Less variables?
questions.answer:
**Sass variables are compiled away at build time into fixed values. CSS custom properties live in the browser at runtime: they cascade, inherit, can be changed per element, by media queries or by JavaScript, and every use updates live.**

| | Sass `$var` | CSS `--var` |
|---|---|---|
| Resolved | Build time | Runtime, per element |
| Scope | Lexical (file/block) | DOM tree, inherited |
| Change with media query / JS | No | Yes |
| Works in `calc()` at runtime | No | Yes |

```css
:root { --accent: oklch(62% 0.19 255); --space: 1rem; }
[data-theme="dark"] { --accent: oklch(75% 0.15 255); }

.btn { background: var(--accent); padding: var(--space) calc(var(--space) * 2); }
.btn.small { --space: .5rem; }  /* override scoped to this element */
```

```js
document.documentElement.style.setProperty("--accent", "tomato");
```

**What this enables:** theming and dark mode by swapping a few variables, component APIs (`--card-padding`), and passing values from JS (scroll progress, pointer position) without touching each rule. Design-token systems and shadcn/ui themes are built on this.

**@property** registers a typed custom property so it can be animated and has a fallback:

```css
@property --angle { syntax: "<angle>"; inherits: false; initial-value: 0deg; }
```

**Gotchas**
- Custom properties are invalid-at-computed-value-time: a bad value makes the property fall back to `inherit`/`initial`, not to the previous declaration.
- They cannot be used in media query conditions or selectors.
- Sass still has a place for mixins, loops and build-time math, but native nesting and custom properties cover most of what people used it for.
followUps: How would you implement a dark mode with custom properties?
Why can't you animate an unregistered custom property smoothly?
What does var(--x, fallback) do?
mistakes: Thinking custom properties are just a native copy of Sass variables.
Not knowing they inherit through the DOM.
Expecting them to work inside media query conditions.

questions.q: Walk through how a browser renders a page. Which CSS properties are cheap to animate and why?
questions.answer:
**The browser parses HTML into the DOM and CSS into the CSSOM, combines them into a render tree, computes layout (geometry), paints pixels into layers, and composites the layers on the GPU. Animating `transform` and `opacity` is cheap because they only need compositing; animating `width`, `top` or `margin` triggers layout and paint every frame.**

**The pipeline**
1. **Parse:** HTML to DOM, CSS to CSSOM. CSS is render-blocking; classic scripts are parser-blocking.
2. **Style:** match selectors and compute each element's final values.
3. **Layout (reflow):** compute size and position of every box.
4. **Paint:** fill in pixels: text, colours, borders, shadows, into one or more layers.
5. **Composite:** the GPU stacks layers, applying transforms and opacity.

**Cost of a change**
- **Layout properties** (`width`, `height`, `top`, `margin`, `font-size`): layout, paint, composite. Expensive and can cascade to the whole page.
- **Paint-only** (`color`, `background`, `box-shadow`): paint and composite.
- **Composite-only** (`transform`, `opacity`, `filter` on a promoted layer): can run on the compositor thread, smooth even if the main thread is busy.

```css
/* Janky */
.panel { transition: left .3s; }
.panel.open { left: 0; }

/* Smooth */
.panel { transition: transform .3s; transform: translateX(-100%); }
.panel.open { transform: translateX(0); }
```

**Layout thrashing:** reading layout (`offsetHeight`, `getBoundingClientRect`) after writing styles forces synchronous layout. In a loop that is one forced layout per iteration; batch reads, then writes, or use `requestAnimationFrame`.

**Gotchas**
- `will-change: transform` promotes a layer up front, but each layer costs GPU memory; add it only where needed.
- `content-visibility: auto` skips rendering off-screen sections, a big win for long pages.
- Measure with the DevTools Performance panel instead of guessing.
followUps: What is layout thrashing and how do you avoid it?
What does content-visibility: auto do?
Why is CSS render-blocking and how can you reduce its impact?
mistakes: Saying all animations are GPU accelerated.
Not distinguishing layout, paint and composite costs.
Overusing will-change on everything.

questions.q: What is the difference between a normal script, defer, async and type="module"?
questions.answer:
**A plain classic script tag blocks HTML parsing while it downloads and runs. `defer` downloads in parallel and runs after parsing, in document order. `async` downloads in parallel and runs as soon as it arrives, in any order. `type="module"` scripts are deferred by default.**

```html
<script src="a.js"></script>                 <!-- blocks parser -->
<script src="app.js" defer></script>          <!-- after parse, in order -->
<script src="analytics.js" async></script>    <!-- whenever ready, unordered -->
<script type="module" src="main.js"></script> <!-- deferred, strict mode -->
```

**Timeline**
- **Classic:** parse, stop, fetch, execute, resume parsing. This is why scripts used to go at the end of `<body>`.
- **defer:** fetch during parsing; execute after the document is parsed, just before `DOMContentLoaded`, preserving order. Best default for app code that touches the DOM.
- **async:** fetch during parsing; execute immediately when downloaded, pausing the parser at that moment. Order is not guaranteed. Good for independent scripts like analytics or ads.
- **module:** deferred by default, strict mode, its own scope, imports fetched as a graph. Adding `async` makes it run as soon as its graph is ready. Inline module scripts are deferred too; inline classic scripts ignore `defer`.

**Related tools**
- `<link rel="preload" as="script">` fetches early without executing.
- `<link rel="modulepreload">` preloads a module and its dependencies.
- `fetchpriority="high"` / `"low"` hints how important a resource is.

**Gotchas**
- Two `async` scripts where one depends on the other will break randomly.
- `defer` does not delay past `load`; it runs before `DOMContentLoaded`.
- A classic script placed after a stylesheet waits for that CSS to load, because the script might read styles.
followUps: When does DOMContentLoaded fire relative to deferred scripts?
Why might an async analytics script still hurt performance?
What is the difference between preload and prefetch?
mistakes: Saying async preserves execution order.
Not knowing module scripts are deferred by default.
Thinking defer works on inline classic scripts.

questions.q: How do HTML and CSS choices affect Core Web Vitals like LCP and CLS, and how would you fix a page with bad layout shift?
questions.answer: **Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) comes from content moving after it first renders, usually images without dimensions, late-loading fonts, ads or banners injected above content. Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) is about how fast the main hero content appears, which HTML controls through resource discovery and priority. Both are mostly fixed in markup and CSS, not JavaScript.** **Fixing CLS** - **Reserve space for media:** always set `width` and `height` attributes (the browser derives an aspect ratio) or use `aspect-ratio` in CSS. - **Reserve space for dynamic slots:** ads, embeds and cookie banners get a fixed `min-height`, or overlay the page instead of pushing it. - **Fonts:** use `font-display: swap` plus a metric-matched fallback (`size-adjust`, `ascent-override`) so the swap does not reflow text; preload the main font. - **Animate with transform**, never `top`/`height`, for things that move after load. - **Skeletons** should match the final size of the content. ```html ``` ```css .embed { aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; width: 100%; } @font-face { font-family: "Brand Fallback"; src: local("Arial"); size-adjust: 105%; ascent-override: 92%; } ``` **Fixing LCP** - Make the hero image discoverable in the HTML (not a CSS background or JS-injected), give it `fetchpriority="high"`, and never lazy-load it. - Serve modern formats with `srcset`/`sizes` so phones do not download desktop images. - Inline critical CSS or keep CSS small; defer non-critical scripts. - Server-render the main content so it does not wait for JavaScript. **How to debug:** the Performance panel's Layout Shift track and the Web Vitals extension show which element moved and why; field data (CrUX, RUM) matters more than one lab run, since CLS often happens on slow connections or during scroll.
followUps: Why does loading="lazy" on the hero image hurt LCP?
What does INP measure and what usually causes a bad score?
How does font-display: swap cause layout shift, and how do you prevent it?
mistakes: Lazy-loading the LCP image.
Omitting width and height on images because CSS makes them responsive.
Only measuring in lab tools and ignoring field data.

questions.q: How do landmarks and the heading outline help screen-reader users, and how would you structure a typical page?
questions.answer:
**Screen-reader users rarely read a page top to bottom: they jump between landmarks (banner, navigation, main, footer) and skim the list of headings. Landmark elements and a ranked h1 to h6 outline give them that map, so I structure every page as header, labelled nav, one main, optional aside, footer, with one h1 and properly nested headings.** **How it works** Sectioning elements map to landmark roles in the accessibility tree: `header` to banner and `footer` to contentinfo (when not nested inside article, aside, main, nav or section), `nav` to navigation, `main` to main, `aside` to complementary, and `section` or `form` to region or form only when they have an accessible name. Screen readers expose these as a landmarks menu (VoiceOver rotor, NVDA's D key) and headings as a separate list (H key, Insert+F7). ```html Skip to content
Acme
...

Pricing

Plans

Team

...
...
``` **Rules I follow** - Exactly one visible `main`; a skip link to it for keyboard users. - Label duplicate landmarks (`aria-label="Primary"`, `"Footer"`), otherwise the menu shows two identical "navigation" entries. - Headings by rank, not size: one h1, h2 for sections, no skipped levels going down. Visual size comes from classes. - Do not wrap everything in `section`; an unnamed section is just a div, and too many landmarks are noise. **A myth worth naming** The HTML5 outline algorithm, where each section resets heading levels so you could use h1 everywhere, was never implemented by browsers or assistive tech and was removed from the spec in 2022. Nested h1s are a flat list of level-1 headings. **Verifying it**: the axe extension flags missing main or duplicate unlabelled landmarks; a headings-map extension or the screen reader's headings list shows whether the outline reads like a table of contents. On a real redesign, adding landmarks and fixing heading order is often the cheapest large accessibility improvement on the page.
followUps: When does a section element become a landmark?
Was the HTML5 document outline algorithm ever implemented?
How do you label two nav elements on one page?
mistakes: Weak answers miss that screen-reader users navigate by landmarks and headings rather than reading top to bottom.
Choosing heading levels for font size, or using an h1 in every section expecting the outline algorithm to fix levels.
Adding unlabelled duplicate landmarks or wrapping everything in section elements.

questions.q: Why should a clickable control be a button rather than a div with a click handler?
questions.answer:
**Because a native button comes with behaviour that a div does not: it is focusable, activates on Enter and Space, is announced as a button with a disabled state, works with forms and respects platform features like high-contrast mode. A div with a click handler only works for mouse users unless you rebuild all of that, and ARIA only changes the announcement, not the behaviour.** **What the div is missing** - **Focus**: not in the tab order without `tabindex="0"`. - **Keyboard**: no Enter or Space activation. Real buttons fire on Enter at keydown and on Space at keyup, and Space must not scroll the page. - **Semantics**: announced as nothing (or "group") without `role="button"`. - **State**: `disabled` blocks clicks and focus and matches `:disabled`; a div needs `aria-disabled` plus guards in every handler. - **Forms**: buttons submit or reset forms and send their name and value. ```tsx // The hand-rolled version, and it is still incomplete
{ if (e.key === "Enter") save(); if (e.key === " ") e.preventDefault(); }} onKeyUp={(e) => { if (e.key === " ") save(); }}> Save
// The native version ``` **Links versus buttons** If it navigates to a URL, it is an `a href` (middle-click, copy link, history and the URL preview all work). If it performs an action on the page, it is a `button`. An anchor with `href="#"` and a click handler is announced as a link, adds a history jump, and breaks expectations. **Gotchas with real buttons** - Inside a form, `button` defaults to `type="submit"`; non-submit buttons need `type="button"`. - Reset styles with `all: unset` or `appearance: none` if needed, but keep a visible `:focus-visible` outline. - Icon-only buttons need a name: `aria-label` or visually hidden text, with the icon `aria-hidden`. **The rule behind it** is the first rule of ARIA: if a native element provides the semantics and behaviour you need, use it. Replacing clickable divs with buttons commonly fixes a batch of audit findings at once.
followUps: What does role="button" add, and what does it not add?
When should a control be a link instead of a button?
Why does a button inside a form submit it by default?
mistakes: Weak answers miss keyboard behaviour: a div is not focusable and does not activate on Enter or Space.
Believing role="button" alone makes a div equivalent to a button.
Using an anchor with href="#" as a button.

questions.q: How do you calculate the specificity of a selector like #nav .item a:hover, and how do :is(), :where() and :not() change it?
questions.answer:
**Specificity is a three-part tuple (ids, classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, types/pseudo-elements) compared left to right. `#nav .item a:hover` is (1, 2, 1). `:is()`, `:not()` and `:has()` take the specificity of their most specific argument, while `:where()` always counts as zero.**

**Counting**
- A column: id selectors.
- B column: classes, attribute selectors (`[type="text"]`), pseudo-classes (`:hover`, `:focus-visible`, `:nth-child()`).
- C column: type selectors (`a`, `li`) and pseudo-elements (`::before`).
- `*`, combinators (`>`, `+`, `~`, space) add nothing.

`#nav .item a:hover`: one id, `.item` plus `:hover` in B, `a` in C, so (1, 2, 1). Compare column by column: one id beats any number of classes, because it is not base-10. (0, 11, 0) loses to (1, 0, 0).

**Functional pseudo-classes**
```css
:is(#hero, .card) p   { }  /* (1,0,1) even when it matched via .card */
:not(.active)         { }  /* (0,1,0) */
.list :where(li, dd)  { }  /* (0,1,0): :where adds nothing */
a:has(> svg)          { }  /* (0,0,2) */
```
That `:is()` behaviour surprises people: one id in the list raises the whole selector. It also matters for native CSS nesting, which wraps the parent selector list in `:is()`.

`:where()` is the tool for library and reset defaults: everything overrides them without escalation.

**Where specificity sits in the cascade**
Specificity is only consulted after origin and importance, inline `style` attributes, and cascade layers. A low-specificity rule in a later `@layer` beats an id selector in an earlier layer. Source order is the final tiebreak.

**In practice** keep selectors flat (single classes) so specificity rarely decides anything, use layers for precedence between groups of CSS, and avoid ids for styling. In Chromium DevTools, hovering a selector shows its specificity tuple, which settles arguments quickly.
followUps: Do 11 classes beat one id?
Where do cascade layers sit relative to specificity?
How would you write library defaults that are easy to override?
mistakes: Weak answers miss that specificity is a tuple compared column by column, not a base-10 number.
Thinking :is() adds nothing, or that :where() takes its argument's specificity.
Forgetting that inline styles and layers are decided before specificity.

questions.q: Explain inheritance in CSS and the difference between inherit, initial, unset, revert and revert-layer.
questions.answer:
**When no declaration sets a property on an element, inherited properties (mostly text ones like color, font and line-height, plus custom properties) take the parent's computed value, and everything else takes its initial value from the spec. The keywords let you choose explicitly: inherit copies the parent, initial uses the spec's initial value, unset does whichever is natural for that property, revert rolls back to the browser's or user's stylesheet, and revert-layer rolls back to the previous cascade layer.**

**What inherits**
- Inherited: `color`, `font-*`, `line-height`, `letter-spacing`, `text-align`, `white-space`, `visibility`, `cursor`, `list-style`, and all custom properties.
- Not inherited: `margin`, `padding`, `border`, `background`, `width`, `height`, `display`, `position`, `opacity`, `transform`.

That is why setting `font-family` on `body` styles the whole page but `padding` does not cascade into children.

**The keywords**
| Keyword | Result |
|---|---|
| `inherit` | Parent's computed value, even for non-inherited properties (`border: inherit`) |
| `initial` | The property's initial value from the spec |
| `unset` | `inherit` for inherited properties, `initial` otherwise |
| `revert` | The value from the previous origin, usually the browser default stylesheet |
| `revert-layer` | The value from the previous cascade layer (or origin if none) |

**The classic trap**
```css
div { display: initial; }   /* inline! initial value of display is inline */
div { display: revert; }    /* block: the UA stylesheet value */
```
`initial` ignores the browser stylesheet; `revert` respects it. Likewise `color: initial` is usually black (CanvasText), not your theme colour.

**Useful patterns**
- `button { font: inherit; color: inherit; }` because form controls do not inherit fonts by default in UA styles.
- `all: revert` on a widget root to drop page styles leaking in (for example inside a CMS).
- `revert-layer` in a utilities layer to fall back to the component's value instead of hard-coding it.
- Custom properties inherit, which is why themes work: set `--color-fg` on a container and every descendant sees it.

**Debugging**: the Computed pane in DevTools shows "inherited from" sections, which tells you exactly which ancestor supplied a value.
followUps: Why does display: initial make a div inline?
Do custom properties inherit?
What does all: revert do on a component root?
mistakes: Weak answers miss which properties inherit (mostly text-related) and which do not (box-related).
Confusing initial (the spec's initial value) with the browser's default stylesheet value, which is what revert gives.
Not knowing revert-layer exists or what it rolls back to.

questions.q: What does flex: 1 actually mean, and why does a flex item sometimes refuse to shrink below its content?
questions.answer:
**`flex: 1` expands to `flex: 1 1 0%`: grow factor 1, shrink factor 1, basis zero. Because the basis is zero, all the space is treated as free space and shared equally, so siblings with flex: 1 end up equal width. An item refuses to shrink below its content because flex items default to min-width: auto, which resolves to their min-content size; setting min-width: 0 fixes it.**

**The shorthands**
| Value | Expands to | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| default | `0 1 auto` | content-sized, can shrink, will not grow |
| `flex: 1` | `1 1 0%` | equal shares of the container |
| `flex: auto` | `1 1 auto` | content size plus a share of leftover space |
| `flex: none` | `0 0 auto` | rigid |

**How the algorithm uses them**
```text
1. base size = flex-basis (or content size when basis is auto)
2. free space = container - sum(base sizes) - gaps
3. free > 0: distribute by flex-grow
   free < 0: remove by flex-shrink x base size (big items shrink more)
4. clamp each item by min/max width; redistribute if clamped
```
Step 4 is where the surprise lives. With `min-width: auto`, the minimum is the min-content width, so a long unbreakable string stops the item shrinking and the row overflows the viewport.

```css
.layout { display: flex; }
.layout > main { flex: 1; min-width: 0; }   /* allow shrinking */
.layout pre { overflow-x: auto; }           /* then contain the overflow */
.layout .url { overflow-wrap: anywhere; }
```

Grid has the same issue: `1fr` means `minmax(auto, 1fr)`, so write `minmax(0, 1fr)` when a column must be allowed to shrink.

**Even "equal" can be unequal**: with `flex: 1`, an item whose min-content is wider than its share still grows to its min-content width, so columns differ. `min-width: 0` restores equality (and pushes overflow inside).

**Real-world example**: chat apps with a sidebar and a message column regularly hit this when someone pastes a long link; the message pane widens and a horizontal scrollbar appears on the whole page. The one-line fix is `min-width: 0` on the column.
followUps: What is the difference between flex: 1 and flex: auto?
Does the same problem happen with 1fr in grid?
How is flex-shrink weighted?
mistakes: Weak answers miss that flex: 1 sets flex-basis to 0%, which is why items become equal.
Not knowing that min-width: auto resolves to min-content for flex items.
Fixing overflow with overflow: hidden on the page instead of min-width: 0 on the item.

questions.q: How does repeat(auto-fit, minmax(240px, 1fr)) work, and how is auto-fit different from auto-fill?
questions.answer:
**`repeat(auto-fit, minmax(240px, 1fr))` asks the grid to create as many columns as fit, each at least 240px and at most an equal share of the row, so the number of columns changes with the container width without media queries. auto-fill and auto-fit both create as many tracks as fit; the difference is that auto-fill keeps empty tracks while auto-fit collapses them, so with few items auto-fit stretches them across the row.**

**Step by step at 1000px wide, gap 16px**
```text
how many 240px tracks fit?   floor((1000 + 16) / (240 + 16)) = 3
three tracks, then 1fr shares the leftover: each (1000 - 32) / 3 = ~322px
at 700px: 2 tracks of ~342px; at 400px: 1 track of 400px
```

**auto-fill versus auto-fit with only two items at 1200px**
```text
auto-fill:  [item][item][    ][    ]   empty tracks kept, items stay ~290px
auto-fit:   [   item   ][   item   ]   empty tracks collapse to 0, items stretch
```
They behave identically once there are enough items to fill the row. Use **auto-fill** when cards should keep a consistent width regardless of count (a product grid with one search result should not show one giant card); **auto-fit** when items should fill the row.

**The narrow-screen bug**
If the container is narrower than 240px (a 320px phone with padding), the single track still demands 240px and overflows. Guard the minimum:
```css
.cards {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(240px, 100%), 1fr));
  gap: 1rem;
}
```

**Compared with flex-wrap**
`flex-wrap` with `flex: 1 1 240px` also wraps, but each line is sized independently, so a last row with one item stretches to full width and columns do not align between rows. Grid keeps columns aligned across rows, which is usually what a gallery wants.

**Limits**: it responds to the container's width, not to content or the item count beyond what fits, and the breakpoints are implicit. When a component needs a different internal layout at certain widths, combine it with container queries on the cards.
followUps: Why wrap the minimum in min(240px, 100%)?
When would you prefer auto-fill?
How is this different from flex-wrap?
mistakes: Weak answers miss that the difference only shows when there are fewer items than tracks.
Forgetting the overflow on screens narrower than the minimum track size.
Claiming this needs media queries to be responsive.

questions.q: What does the viewport meta tag do, and why does a site look zoomed out on phones without it?
questions.answer:
**`<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">` tells mobile browsers to make the layout viewport as wide as the device in CSS pixels. Without it, browsers assume a desktop site, lay the page out on a wide virtual viewport (980px on iOS Safari) and then zoom out to fit, so text is tiny and your media queries see 980px and never fire.**

**Two viewports**
```text
layout viewport: the width CSS lays out against (what media queries and vw see)
visual viewport: the part currently visible on screen (changes with pinch-zoom and the keyboard)

without the tag:  layout = 980px  -> page scaled down to fit a 390px screen
with the tag:     layout = 390px  -> 1 CSS px is roughly 1 device-independent px, no scaling
```
`initial-scale=1` sets the starting zoom to 100%, which also avoids some orientation-change zoom quirks.

**What not to add**
`maximum-scale=1` or `user-scalable=no` blocks pinch-zoom. Low-vision users rely on zoom, so this fails WCAG 1.4.4 (resize text) and 1.4.10 (reflow) expectations. iOS Safari ignores these values by default for accessibility reasons, but other browsers honour them. A common reason people add them is to stop iOS zooming into inputs on focus; the right fix is a font size of at least 16px on inputs.

**What the tag does not do**
It does not make a layout responsive. It just gives your responsive CSS the correct width to respond to. You still need fluid layouts, rem-based breakpoints and responsive images.

**Related details**
- `interactive-widget=resizes-content` controls whether the on-screen keyboard resizes the layout viewport, which matters for chat inputs pinned to the bottom (check browser support).
- `viewport-fit=cover` plus `env(safe-area-inset-*)` handles notches when you draw edge to edge.
- In Next.js, the viewport is configured through the `viewport` export in a layout rather than a hand-written tag, and the default already includes `width=device-width, initial-scale=1`.
followUps: Why should you not set user-scalable=no?
What is the difference between the layout and visual viewport?
Why use rem in media queries?
mistakes: Weak answers miss the layout viewport: without the tag, mobile browsers lay out at about 980px and scale down.
Recommending maximum-scale=1 or user-scalable=no, which blocks zoom and fails WCAG 1.4.4.
Thinking the tag itself makes a layout responsive.

questions.q: How do srcset, sizes and the picture element work for responsive images?
questions.answer: **`srcset` lists the same image at several widths and `sizes` tells the browser how wide the image will render, so it can pick the smallest file that is sharp enough for that slot and the device pixel ratio. `picture` with `source` elements is for the cases srcset cannot handle: art direction (a different crop per breakpoint) and format fallbacks such as AVIF, then WebP, then JPEG.** **Resolution switching** ```html ``` The browser evaluates `sizes` (first matching condition wins) to get the slot width, multiplies by the device pixel ratio, and picks a candidate: a 390px-wide phone at DPR 3 needs about 1170 device pixels, so it takes the 1920w file. It may choose differently (for example a smaller file on a constrained connection), so these are hints. **If you omit sizes it defaults to 100vw**, which makes a 300px thumbnail download a full-width file. **Art direction and formats** ```html ``` The first matching `source` wins; the img element is required, carries `alt`, sizing and loading attributes, and is what actually renders. **Core Web Vitals details** - **width and height attributes** let the browser compute the aspect ratio before download and reserve space, preventing layout shift (CLS). Use CSS `max-width: 100%; height: auto` to keep it fluid. - **Never lazy-load the LCP image**; give it `fetchpriority="high"`. Use `loading="lazy"` for below-the-fold images. - Framework components (Next.js `Image`, Astro's image tools) generate srcset and sizes for you, but you still have to supply a correct `sizes` for non-full-width images. **Pixel density descriptors** (`1x`, `2x`) suit fixed-size images such as logos; width descriptors suit fluid images.
followUps: What happens if you omit sizes?
Why set width and height attributes on a responsive image?
Should the LCP image be lazy-loaded?
mistakes: Weak answers miss that sizes defaults to 100vw, which wastes bytes on small slots.
Using picture with media sources when srcset alone would do (picture is for art direction and formats).
Lazy-loading the hero image, which delays LCP.

questions.q: How do you build fluid typography with clamp() without breaking zoom accessibility?
questions.answer:
**I use clamp(min, preferred, max) where the preferred value mixes rem and vw, for example clamp(1rem, 0.9rem + 0.5vw, 1.25rem), so text scales smoothly between two viewport widths. The rem part is what keeps it accessible: a pure vw size ignores browser zoom and the user's default font size, which can fail WCAG 1.4.4 (resize text to 200%).**

**Deriving the value**
Pick a minimum size at a minimum viewport and a maximum size at a maximum viewport, then solve the line between them:
```text
min: 1rem (16px) at 360px     max: 1.25rem (20px) at 1280px
slope     = (20 - 16) / (1280 - 360) = 0.004348 per px  -> 0.4348vw
intercept = 16 - 0.004348 * 360 = 14.43px              -> 0.902rem
result: font-size: clamp(1rem, 0.902rem + 0.435vw, 1.25rem);
```
Tools like Utopia generate a whole type and spacing scale this way, which keeps headings, body text and spacing in proportion.

**Why the rem term matters**
When a user zooms the page, CSS pixels get bigger but the viewport in CSS pixels gets narrower, so `4vw` text stays the same physical size on screen. A rem term grows with zoom and with the browser's default font-size setting. Two more rules:
- Express min and max in rem, not px, so they follow user preferences.
- Keep the max-to-min ratio moderate (about 2.5x or less). If the max is far larger than the min, zooming to 200% may not double the text, because the vw component shrinks as the layout viewport narrows.

```css
:root {
  --step-0: clamp(1rem, 0.9rem + 0.43vw, 1.25rem);
  --step-2: clamp(1.44rem, 1.2rem + 1.1vw, 2.1rem);
  --step-4: clamp(2.07rem, 1.5rem + 2.6vw, 3.6rem);
}
h1 { font-size: var(--step-4); text-wrap: balance; }
```

**Container query units** (`cqi`) are great for component-level fluid type (a card title that scales with its card), with the same rule: combine them with rem.

**Testing**: zoom to 200% in a desktop browser and confirm body text roughly doubles; set the browser's default font size to 20px and confirm the page grows; check line length stays near 45 to 75 characters (`max-inline-size: 65ch`).
followUps: How do you derive the slope and intercept for a clamp() value?
Why might a large max-to-min ratio fail WCAG 1.4.4?
Would you use container query units for type?
mistakes: Weak answers miss that pure vw font sizes do not respond to zoom or the user's default font size.
Using px for the min and max, ignoring user font preferences.
Not testing at 200% zoom.

questions.q: How does the View Transitions API work, and what are its limits?
questions.answer:
**The browser snapshots the current state, runs your DOM update, captures the new state, then animates between them using pseudo-elements in the top layer: by default the old view cross-fades into the new, and elements given the same view-transition-name morph in position and size. Limits: names must be unique at capture time, the old view is a static image, interaction is blocked during the transition, and cross-document support is narrower than same-document support.**

**Same-document**
```js
function go(update) {
  if (!document.startViewTransition) { update(); return; }   // fallback
  const t = document.startViewTransition(() => update());     // update may be async
  return t.finished;
}
```
```css
.card-thumb.active { view-transition-name: hero; }   /* old view */
.detail-hero       { view-transition-name: hero; }   /* new view */
::view-transition-group(hero) { animation-duration: 250ms; }
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  ::view-transition-group(*), ::view-transition-old(*), ::view-transition-new(*) { animation: none; }
}
```
```text
::view-transition
  ::view-transition-group(root | hero)      animates size and position
    ::view-transition-image-pair(hero)
      ::view-transition-old(hero)           static snapshot, fades out
      ::view-transition-new(hero)           live content, fades in
```
The returned object exposes `ready`, `updateCallbackDone` and `finished` promises and `skipTransition()`. You can drive custom animations with the Web Animations API once `ready` resolves.

**Cross-document (MPA)**
Both pages opt in with `@view-transition { navigation: auto; }`; navigations must be same-origin. `pageswap` and `pagereveal` events let you set names dynamically. Chromium and Safari support it; check current Firefox support and treat it as an enhancement.

**Limits and gotchas**
- Duplicate `view-transition-name`s abort the transition. Assign the name only to the clicked item.
- The old snapshot is frozen: videos or animations inside it stop during the transition.
- Pointer events are blocked while it runs, so keep transitions short (200 to 300ms).
- Aspect-ratio changes between old and new images can look stretched; adjust with `object-fit` on the old and new pseudo-elements.
- Long DOM updates delay the transition; if the callback is slow, the page appears frozen.

**Real use**: list-to-detail morphs, tab switches and theme toggles in SPAs. React and Next.js have been adding first-class integrations, so check your framework's documentation before wiring it by hand.
followUps: How do you opt into cross-document view transitions?

mistakes: Weak answers miss that the old state is a static snapshot and the new state is live.
Forgetting feature detection and a plain fallback.
Assigning the same view-transition-name to many elements, which aborts the transition.

questions.q: What are CSS logical properties, and why would you use margin-inline-start instead of margin-left?
questions.answer:
**Logical properties describe sides in terms of the text flow (block and inline, start and end) rather than physical directions (top, right, bottom, left). margin-inline-start means "before the text in the reading direction": left in English, right in Arabic or Hebrew, top in vertical writing modes. Using them means a layout mirrors correctly when you set dir="rtl" or change writing-mode, with no extra CSS.**

**Vocabulary**
```text
horizontal-tb, ltr (English):    inline axis = left to right, block axis = top to bottom
horizontal-tb, rtl (Arabic):     inline axis = right to left
vertical-rl (Japanese vertical): inline axis = top to bottom, block axis = right to left
```
| Physical | Logical |
|---|---|
| `width`, `height` | `inline-size`, `block-size` |
| `margin-left`, `margin-right` | `margin-inline-start`, `margin-inline-end` |
| `padding-top` and `padding-bottom` | `padding-block` |
| `top`, `left` | `inset-block-start`, `inset-inline-start` |
| `border-top-left-radius` | `border-start-start-radius` |
| `text-align: left` | `text-align: start` |
| `float: left` | `float: inline-start` |

**Example**
```css
.notice {
  border-inline-start: 4px solid var(--color-warning);
  padding-inline: 1rem 0.75rem;
  margin-block-end: 1.5rem;
}
.icon { margin-inline-end: 0.5rem; }
```
With `dir="rtl"` on the html element, the accent border moves to the right and the icon gap flips, automatically.

**Why use them even for an English-only site**
- The shorthands are terser: `margin-inline: auto`, `padding-block: 1rem`, `inset: 0`.
- Internationalisation later costs nothing instead of a CSS audit.
- Components in a shared design system may be used by teams that do localise.

**Things to know**
- Flexbox and grid already follow direction: `justify-content: flex-start` and grid column 1 start on the right in RTL. Physical margins inside them are what break.
- Transforms (`translateX`) and background positions are physical; flip them with a `:dir(rtl)` rule where needed.
- Do not mix physical and logical properties for the same side in one rule set; whichever comes later wins and the result depends on direction, which is confusing.
- Icons with direction (arrows, back buttons) need mirroring; icons like a clock or a checkmark should not be mirrored.
followUps: What do block and inline mean in a vertical writing mode?

mistakes: Weak answers miss writing modes and only mention RTL.
Mixing physical and logical properties for the same side and getting conflicting values.
Thinking flex and grid need extra CSS for RTL; they already follow direction.

questions.q: Compare BEM, CSS Modules, Tailwind and CSS-in-JS. Which would you pick for a large React app and why?
questions.answer:
**They differ in how styles are scoped and when CSS is produced. BEM is a naming convention with no tooling; CSS Modules hash class names at build time; Tailwind generates only the utility classes you use; runtime CSS-in-JS generates and injects styles during render. For a large React app on Server Components I would pick Tailwind or CSS Modules on top of a design-token layer, and avoid adding runtime CSS-in-JS.**

**Comparison**
| | Scoping | Runtime cost | RSC fit | Main risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| BEM | Convention only | None | Fine | Naming drift, dead CSS |
| CSS Modules | Hashed classes | None | Fine | Prop-driven variants need class toggling |
| Tailwind | Atomic, no scoping needed | None | Fine | Long class strings, learning curve |
| Runtime CSS-in-JS | Generated classes | Serialise and inject on render | Client components only | Render cost, bundle size |
| Zero-runtime CSS-in-JS | Generated classes | None | Fine | Build complexity |

**How I would decide**
- **Team and design**: Tailwind suits product teams that iterate fast within a defined theme; CSS Modules suit teams that like writing CSS, or designs with complex selectors and animations.
- **Scale**: Tailwind's CSS output plateaus because new pages reuse utilities; CSS Modules grow per component but stay isolated and deletable with the component.
- **Design system**: components expose variants (with a helper like `cva` for Tailwind, or data attributes with CSS Modules), never ask consumers to override internals.
- **Platform**: with RSC and streaming, build-time CSS just works; runtime libraries require client boundaries and style-collection integration.

**What I would put in place regardless**
- Semantic design tokens as CSS custom properties, which Tailwind v4 also exposes from its `@theme`.
- Cascade layers to order reset, vendor, components and utilities.
- One approach per codebase, enforced by lint (Stylelint, a class-sorting plugin, a rule against raw hex colours).
- Readability helpers: extract repeated Tailwind combinations into components, not into `@apply` soup.

**A good answer acknowledges trade-offs**: Tailwind's markup is noisy, and CSS Modules make dynamic styling clunkier. The decision is about the team, the platform and consistency, not about which one is "best".
followUps: How would you keep Tailwind class lists readable?
How do you enforce one approach across many teams?
Where do cascade layers fit in your choice?
mistakes: Weak answers declare a favourite without comparing scoping, runtime cost, RSC fit and team skills.
Ignoring that runtime CSS-in-JS conflicts with Server Components and streaming.
Recommending a mix of several approaches in one codebase.

questions.q: Why has runtime CSS-in-JS fallen out of favour with React Server Components and streaming?
questions.answer:
**Runtime CSS-in-JS libraries such as styled-components and Emotion serialise styles and insert CSS rules while React renders, which costs time on every render and ships the library to the client. They also depend on React context and client-side hooks, so they cannot run in Server Components, and they need special handling to collect and order styles during streaming SSR. Build-time options give the same scoping without those costs, so the ecosystem moved there.**

**Where the cost comes from**
```text
render -> evaluate template with props -> serialise CSS string -> hash it
       -> if new, insert a rule into a style sheet (insertRule)
       -> browser recalculates styles for the document
```
Components whose props change often (a draggable item, a data-grid cell) repeat this work on every update. Sam Magura, then an Emotion maintainer, described measuring this in a production app and finding render times dropped substantially after moving to Sass modules ("Why we're breaking up with CSS-in-JS"). React added `useInsertionEffect` specifically so these libraries could inject styles before layout effects read the DOM, which signals how awkward the model is.

**Server Components and streaming**
- Server Components cannot use context or hooks, so every styled component must sit behind a `"use client"` boundary, which defeats much of the point of RSC.
- With streaming, styles must be collected per chunk and inserted before the HTML that uses them, or users see unstyled content. Libraries need framework-specific registries to do this.
- The JavaScript that generates styles is shipped and executed on the client even for static content.

**The ecosystem response**
- styled-components announced it was entering maintenance mode in 2025.
- Zero-runtime libraries (vanilla-extract, Panda CSS, Linaria, Meta's StyleX) keep typed, colocated styles but extract static CSS at build time. Dynamic values flow through CSS custom properties: `style={{ "--progress": pct }}` plus a static rule using `var(--progress)`.
- Tailwind and CSS Modules became the default choices in new Next.js apps.

**Migrating a large codebase**
1. Stop writing new styled components; establish tokens as CSS custom properties that both systems read.
2. Convert leaf components first (buttons, inputs), keeping their props API stable.
3. Replace theme context lookups with custom properties set on a root attribute.
4. Remove the library and its SSR registry once nothing imports it, and measure bundle size and render time before and after.

questions.q: How do you label form inputs accessibly, and why is a placeholder not a label?
questions.answer:
**Every input needs a visible label that is programmatically associated with it, usually a label element with for pointing at the input's id, or a label wrapping the input. That gives the field its accessible name and makes the label clickable. A placeholder is not a label because it disappears as soon as the user types, usually has low contrast, and is not reliably exposed as the field's name.** ```html

We will send the invoice here.

Delivery speed
``` **What the label gives you** - Accessible name: "Work email, edit text, required". - A larger click and tap target: clicking the label focuses the input or toggles the checkbox. - Voice control: users say "click Work email". **Why placeholders fail as labels** - The text vanishes on input, so users lose context while typing and when reviewing a filled form. - Default placeholder colour often fails contrast requirements, while darkening it makes it look like an entered value. - Screen readers treat it inconsistently as a name. - Placeholder-only fields are a frequent cause of autofill confusion. Use placeholders, if at all, for an example format, and put essential hints in visible text linked with `aria-describedby`. **Other labelling tools** - `aria-labelledby` when the visible label is another element (a table column header labelling inputs in its column). - `aria-label` only when there is truly no visible text (a search field with a clear search button and icon), and make sure the visible icon matches. - Visually hidden labels are acceptable for a search field in a header, but visible labels are better for everyone else. - `fieldset` and `legend` for radio and checkbox groups, so each option is announced with its question. **Floating labels** (label inside the field that moves up on focus) are fine if the label stays visible and readable when filled. **Verifying**: check the computed accessible name in the DevTools accessibility pane, click each label to confirm it focuses its control, and run axe, which flags unlabelled inputs.
followUps: When would you use aria-labelledby instead of a label element?
How do you group radio buttons?
How do you connect hint text to a field?
mistakes: Weak answers miss that placeholder text disappears on input and is not a reliable accessible name.
Using aria-label everywhere instead of visible labels.
Forgetting fieldset and legend for radio and checkbox groups.

questions.q: Which input types and attributes improve form UX on mobile?
questions.answer:
**Pick the input type and inputmode that bring up the right keyboard, add autocomplete tokens so the browser and password managers can fill the form, and use enterkeyhint for the action key. Together they remove most typing on mobile; autocomplete alone is the biggest single win on checkout and login forms.**

**Keyboards**
| Field | Markup |
|---|---|
| Email | `type="email"` (shows @, validates format) |
| Phone | `type="tel"` (phone keypad) |
| OTP, PIN, card number, postcode digits | `type="text" inputmode="numeric" pattern="[0-9]*"` |
| Decimal amount | `type="text" inputmode="decimal"` |
| URL | `type="url"` |
| Search | `type="search"` and `enterkeyhint="search"` |

**Why not type="number" for identifiers**: it drops leading zeros, accepts `e`, changes value on scroll wheel and arrow keys, and screen readers announce it as a spin button. It is meant for quantities.

**Autocomplete tokens**
```html
<input name="name" autocomplete="name">
<input name="email" type="email" autocomplete="email">
<input name="address" autocomplete="street-address">
<input name="zip" inputmode="numeric" autocomplete="postal-code">
<input name="cc" inputmode="numeric" autocomplete="cc-number">
<input name="code" inputmode="numeric" autocomplete="one-time-code">
<input name="pw" type="password" autocomplete="current-password">   <!-- login -->
<input name="newpw" type="password" autocomplete="new-password">    <!-- sign-up: generate -->
```
`one-time-code` lets iOS and Android offer the code from an incoming SMS. `current-password` versus `new-password` tells password managers whether to fill or generate. `autocomplete="off"` on login fields hurts users and is mostly ignored by browsers. WCAG 1.3.5 asks for these tokens on fields that collect the user's own information.

**Other details**
- `enterkeyhint="next" | "done" | "send" | "search"` labels the return key.
- `autocapitalize="off"` and `spellcheck="false"` for usernames and codes; `autocapitalize="words"` for names.
- Inputs with font-size under 16px make iOS Safari zoom in on focus; fix the font size, do not disable zoom.
- Mark up the form as a real `form` with a submit button so the keyboard's Go key submits.
- Large tap targets (WCAG 2.2 minimum 24 by 24 CSS px) and labels above fields so they are not covered by the keyboard.

**Testing**: on a real phone, fill the form with saved autofill data and a password manager, and count taps.
followUps: Why not use type="number" for a credit card number?
What does autocomplete="new-password" tell a password manager?
Why do inputs under 16px zoom in on iOS?
mistakes: Weak answers miss autocomplete tokens, the single biggest win for checkout and login forms.
Using type="number" for identifiers such as ZIP codes, OTPs or card numbers.
Setting autocomplete="off" on login fields.
